recent_posts.title: Are Caches Accessed with a Virtual or Physical Address?
recent_posts.summary: CPU caches can be addressed using virtual addresses, physical addresses, or a combination of both. Four cache addressing schemes exist: PIPT (physically indexed, physically tagged), VIVT (virtually indexed, virtually tagged), PIVT (physically indexed, virtually tagged), and VIPT (virtually indexed, physically tagged). PIPT is robust but slow due to mandatory address translation before cache access. VIVT is fast but suffers from homonym and aliasing problems requiring cache flushes on context switches. PIVT combines the worst of both worlds and is rarely used. VIPT is the modern standard, enabling parallel address translation via the MMU/TLB and cache set lookup using the page offset bits. This parallelism works because the page offset bits remain unchanged during translation. VIPT has constraints: the set index plus line offset bits must not exceed the page offset bits, which is why most L1 caches are limited to 32–64 KB.

recent_posts.title: Why CPUs Have Multiple Cores
recent_posts.summary: A historical explanation of why modern CPUs have multiple cores instead of ever-faster single cores. Covers Moore's Law and Dennard Scaling, which enabled decades of predictable clock frequency growth by shrinking transistors and reducing voltage. Around 2004–2006, this era ended due to the 'power wall': transistors could no longer safely reduce voltage further, and quantum tunneling caused leakage current, making heat dissipation impossible at higher frequencies. This forced a shift in CPU design from single high-frequency cores to multiple medium-speed cores, moving the performance paradigm from latency to throughput and placing the burden of parallelism on software developers.

recent_posts.title: How Out-of-Order Execution Works
recent_posts.summary: Out-of-order execution allows modern processors to execute instructions in a different sequence than program order while maintaining correctness. The technique builds on pipelining and superscalar execution, introducing reservation stations, dispatchers, and reorder buffers to manage instruction flow. Register renaming eliminates false dependencies (write-after-write and write-after-read hazards), while data forwarding reduces stalls from true dependencies. Instructions are broken into micro-operations, executed when inputs are ready, and committed back in original program order through the reorder buffer.

recent_posts.title: How Interrupts Work in Modern Computers
recent_posts.summary: Interrupts are signals that allow hardware devices and the CPU itself to notify the processor when important events occur, eliminating the need for inefficient polling. Hardware interrupts are delivered via IRQ lines or message signaled interrupts (MSI), while software interrupts (exceptions) include faults, traps, and aborts generated by the CPU. When an interrupt occurs, the processor saves the current state, executes the appropriate interrupt service routine (ISR) using an interrupt vector table, and then either restores execution or terminates the process.

recent_posts.title: Why Programs Use Stack, Heap, and Other Memory Segments
recent_posts.summary: Programs use separate memory segments (stack, heap, code, data, BSS) for security, performance, and bug isolation. The stack handles function calls with fast LIFO allocation, while the heap manages dynamic memory allocation. Code segments store executable instructions as read-only, data segments hold initialized variables, and BSS segments contain uninitialized variables. This separation prevents vulnerabilities, optimizes access patterns, and reduces executable file sizes.

recent_posts.title: What is a Page Fault
recent_posts.summary: Page faults are processor exceptions that occur when programs try to access memory not currently loaded in RAM. Modern operating systems use virtual memory organized into pages that can reside in RAM or on disk. When a required page isn't in RAM, the processor triggers a page fault, pausing the program and invoking an interrupt service routine to locate, retrieve, and load the missing page. There are two types: minor page faults (data in RAM but not mapped to virtual memory) and major page faults (data must be loaded from disk). Major page faults significantly impact performance when frequent, while invalid memory access attempts result in segmentation faults that terminate programs.

recent_posts.title: Cache Simulator in C++: Measuring Cache Hit Rate
recent_posts.summary: The post walks through implementing a mechanism to measure cache hit rates in a C++ cache simulator. It introduces a method for calculating hit rates using cache statistics and describes testing scenarios with sequential and random memory reads. The importance of spatial locality in achieving high cache performance is highlighted, with results showing varying hit rates depending on the reading pattern.

top_posts.title: How Virtual Memory Actually Works Behind the Scenes
top_posts.summary: The post explains how virtual memory works behind the scenes, focusing on the structure and function of page tables and the role of the memory management unit (MMU). It covers how page tables are used to map virtual memory to physical memory, the fields within page table entries, and how the MMU manages memory requests and translations. The post also discusses the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) and its function in speeding up address translation.

top_posts.title: Cache Simulator in C++: Building a Basic Framework
top_posts.summary: The post outlines a step-by-step process of building a cache simulator in C++. It covers the creation of various components including main memory, random replacement algorithms, and cache structures. The simulator demonstrates cache operations such as read, write, and management of cache lines, while exploring phenomena like cache thrashing.

top_posts.title: Binary Search Tree in C++: Implementing a Basic Tree (Insert, Search & Inorder Traversal)
top_posts.summary: Learn how to implement a binary search tree in C++ with methods for inserting nodes, searching for values, and performing in-order traversal. The post details the creation of the tree node class, explains the structure of the tree, and demonstrates recursion techniques to handle node insertion and value search. The implementation is tested with sample values to verify its correctness.

top_posts.title: How much Physical Memory does Virtual Memory Require?
top_posts.summary: Virtual memory uses page tables for translating virtual addresses to physical ones, posing memory challenges as computers evolve to larger address spaces. Multi-level page tables help optimize memory usage, creating smaller tables only when necessary and marking unused entries as invalid to conserve memory. Systems use memory management units to streamline the translation process efficiently.
